# UnCut FEM WITH PHT-SPLINES ON UNFITTED T-MESHES

Abstract. We propose a novel unfitted finite element method based on polynomial splines over hierarchical T-meshes (PHT-splines) for elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs) posed on domains whose boundaries are described implicitly by a level-set function. Exploiting the enhanced smoothness of the spline space, we formulate the method by minimizing the _L_<sup>2</sup> residual of the PDE over an extended neighborhood of the physical domain. This formulation allows the method to be implemented entirely on the background mesh using standard element-wise quadrature. It yields a symmetric positive-definite linear system and avoids the geometric construction of curved cut subregions in boundary elements, as well as the associated nontrivial numerical integration. We establish well-posedness of the numerical scheme and derive optimal _a priori_ error estimates in the _H_<sup>1</sup> norm. In addition, we employ a residual-based _a posteriori_ error indicator to guide local adaptive refinement of the hierarchical T-meshes. Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical results and demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed approach.

### 1. Introduction

The numerical solution of partial differential equations (PDEs) defined on complex or evolving domains \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) constitutes a cornerstone of contemporary computational science. Traditionally, finite element analysis relies on _body-fitted_ discretisations, where the triangulation _T<sub>h</sub>_ is constrained to conform to the physical boundary \(\partial\Omega\). While robust for static and simple geometries, this paradigm poses significant computational challenges in realistic scenarios. The construction of high-quality, shape-regular meshes that accommodate high-order approximations is often a prohibitive task, frequently dominating the total computational budget of the simulation pipeline.

This bottleneck is particularly pronounced in multi-query environments, such as shape optimisation, inverse problems, and uncertainty quantification, where the governing PDE must be evaluated over an extensive ensemble of geometric configurations. In these contexts, the overhead of repeated mesh generation and the subsequent verification of mesh validity can eclipse the cost of the linear solvers themselves, impeding the development of fully automated workflows. Furthermore, for time-dependent problems involving moving interfaces or evolving boundaries, classical Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian (ALE) frameworks often suffer from progressive mesh distortion. Maintaining the integrity of the numerical scheme necessitates frequent remeshing and sophisticated field interpolation (projection) between successive grids, processes that are not only computationally intensive but also susceptible to introducing numerical dissipation and compromising stability.

To circumvent these geometric constraints, _unfitted_ finite element methods have emerged as a powerful alternative by effectively decoupling the functional discretisation from the underlying domain geometry. By employing a fixed background mesh _T<sub>h</sub>_ and representing the boundary \(\partial\Omega\) implicitly (e.g., via a level-set function), these methods eliminate the need for body-conforming mesh updates. This framework provides a versatile foundation

Among the disparate unfitted formulations, the Immersed Finite Element Method (IFEM) [22,23], the Extended Finite Element Method (XFEM) [29,34], and the Cut Finite Element Method (CutFEM) [7,9] have gained prominence. Furthermore, the unfitted methods have also been applied to the advection-diffusion equation [28], elliptic equations on hypersurfaces [30], elliptic interface problems [25,31,35], fluid-structure interaction problems [8], shape optimization [21] and time-harmonic wave equations [11,26]. A fundamental challenge inherent in these approaches is the _small cut-cell problem_: when the boundary intersects the background elements arbitrarily, the resulting system can become severely ill-conditioned as the measure of the intersection approaches zero.

Two primary paradigms have been established to restore numerical robustness. The first is the _cell-merging_ strategy, exemplified by the work of Chen et al. [12-14], which algebraically or geometrically aggregates small boundary elements with adjacent interior macro-elements. This approach has been shown to effectively mitigate the _p_-dependence of the condition number in _hp_-FEM settings, ensuring geometric stability. The second paradigm is the _variational stabilisation_ framework, notably the ghost penalty method developed by Burman and co- authors [6,10]. By augmenting the bilinear form with penalisation terms on the face facets of cut elements, this approach restores uniform coercivity and ensures that the condition number remains bounded independently of the interface’s relative position to the mesh. Similar minimal stabilisation techniques have also been extended to Unfitted Isogeometric Analysis (IGA) [4,5] and least-squares Nitsche formulations [20] to preserve optimal convergence rates on trimmed geometries.

Although these methods significantly reduce the need for mesh generation, they also introduce new implementation challenges. In particular, they often require numerical integration over geometrically intricate subregions induced by the intersection between the domain boundary and background elements. This typically necessitates geometric intersection algorithms and specialised quadrature rules, which are computationally expensive and difficult to implement robustly, especially in three dimensions. Moreover, such geometry-dependent quadrature procedures may introduce additional errors that are often not explicitly accounted for in existing error analyses of unfitted finite element methods.

To avoid these difficulties in both implementation and analysis, Duprez and Lozinski proposed a novel fictitious domain approach, referred to as \(\phi\)-FEM [3,17-19], where \(\phi\) denotes the level-set function defining the domain. This formulation belongs to the class of UnCut finite element methods, in which all integrals are evaluated over the full background elements using standard quadrature rules, thereby eliminating the need for geometry-dependent integration procedures. Stability and error estimates for \(\phi\)-FEM have been established for the Poisson equation under the assumption that the stabilisation parameters are chosen sufficiently large, depending on constants arising from trace inequalities, Poincaré inequalities, and inverse estimates. In practice, however, determining appropriate values for these parameters remains challenging for general elliptic problems.

To address the issue of parameter selection, Hu, Li, and Yang [24] proposed a robust, parameter-free least-squares UnCut finite element method that guarantees stability and optimal-order convergence without requiring large stabilisation parameters. However, in order to accommodate standard _C_<sup>0</sup> finite element spaces, their approach is formulated through the minimisation of a discrete _H_<sup>-1</sup>-residual of the governing PDE. While effective, this naturally necessitates a dual (mixed) formulation involving an auxiliary variable, thereby increasing both the algebraic dimension and the computational complexity of the resulting linear system.

Motivated by the need for a more computationally efficient framework, this paper introduces a novel UnCut formulation that leverages the high-order regularity of _C_<sup>1</sup>-continuous PHT-splines [15,33]. By exploiting _C_<sup>1</sup> continuity, we can directly discretise the PDE in its strong form, effectively preserving the parameter-free advantages of the UnCut framework<tbc>

<tbc>while entirely circumventing the need for dual variables or mixed systems. To illustrate this approach, we consider the Poisson problem on a domain \(\overline{\Omega}\subset(0,1)^d\) defined by a _C_<sup>_k_+1</sup> level-set function \(\phi:[0,1]^d\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\), with \(d\in\{2,3\}\), i.e.,

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
-\Delta u=f & \text{in}\Omega=\{\mathbf{x}\in(0,1)^d:\phi(\mathbf{x})<0\}, \\
u=0 & \text{on}\partial\Omega=\{\mathbf{x}\in(0,1)^d:\phi(\mathbf{x})=0\}.
\end{array}\right.\) (1.1)

Specifically, we consider a background hierarchical T-mesh T_<sub>h</sub>_ defined over a computational domain \(\Omega_h\) such that<tbc>

\(\Omega\subset\Omega_h\subset[0,1]^d,\text{dist}(\partial\Omega_h,\partial\Omega)=O(h),\)

<tbc>where _h_ denotes the mesh size. The approximation space is then constructed as<tbc>

\(S_h=\{w_h=\phi_hv_h:v_h\in V_h\},\)

<tbc>where _V<sub>h</sub>_ is the discrete spline space defined in (2.2), and \(\phi_h\in V_h\) is a _k_-th degree PHT-spline approximation of \(\phi\) such that

\(\|\phi-\phi_h\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}\le Ch^{k+1},\|\phi-\phi_h\|_{H^1(\Omega_h)}\le Ch^k,\)

for a constant _C\>_0 (e.g., \(\phi_h\) may be chosen as the global spline interpolant or the _L_<sup>2</sup>- projection of \(\phi\)). By construction, every function in _S<sub>h</sub>_ vanishes on the discrete interface \(\Gamma_h=\{\phi_h=0\}\). Thus, the homogeneous Dirichlet condition is imposed exactly on \(\Gamma_h\) and only approximately on the physical boundary \(\Gamma=\partial\Omega\).

We define the numerical solution _u<sub>h</sub>_ to problem (1.1) as the minimizer of the following functional:

\(u_h=argmin_{w_h\in S_h}\left(\|\Delta w_h+f\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}^2+j_h(w_h,w_h)\right),\) (1.2)

where \(j_h(\cdot,\cdot)\) is a jump-type stabilization term defined in (2.6). For simplicity, _f_ is understood as a fixed bounded extension to \(\widehat{\Omega}\), still denoted by _f_. This quadratic minimization problem is equivalent to the following weak formulation: find \(u_h\in S_h\) such that

\((\Delta u_h,\Delta v_h)_{L^2(\Omega_h)}+j_h(u_h,v_h)=-(f,\Delta v_h)_{L^2(\Omega_h)}\forall v_h\in S_h.\) (1.3)

This formulation is used for practical implementation. However, the optimal-order _H_<sup>1</sup> convergence of this scheme--based on minimizing an _L_<sup>2</sup>-residual over a _C_<sup>1</sup> finite element space-- is not immediate and requires careful analysis.

The main contributions of this paper are threefold:

\(\bullet\) _tion:_ We introduce a novel unfitted finite element method in which no numerical integration over curved boundaries or cut subregions of boundary elements is required. All computations are performed on the _entire_ background mesh using standard element-wise quadrature. This is achieved without introducing dual formulations or auxiliary unknowns; instead, we exploit _C_<sup>1</sup> trial spaces constructed via PHT-splines, leading to a method that is both simple to implement and computationally efficient.<tbc>

\(\bullet\) _Theory:_ We establish a rigorous error analysis for the proposed method. In particular, we prove existence and uniqueness of the discrete solution and derive optimal- order error estimates in the _H_<sup>1</sup> norm. This is nontrivial since the formulation is based on minimizing the _L_<sup>2</sup> residual rather than directly enforcing an _H_<sup>1</sup>-coercive variational structure.<tbc>

\(\bullet\) _Adaptivity:_ PHT-splines are defined on hierarchical T-meshes that admit T-junctions, enabling efficient local _h_-refinement via a simple _cross-insertion_ strategy. Leveraging this flexibility, we introduce a residual-based _a posteriori_ error indicator for each cell \(T\in\mathcal{T}_h\),<tbc>

<tbc>\(\eta_T:=\|\Delta u_h+f\|_{L^2(T)},\)<tbc>

and demonstrate through numerical experiments that it provides an effective refinement criterion on hierarchical T-meshes. The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 introduces the hierarchical T-spline spaces and presents the proposed least-squares UnCut FEM scheme. Section 3 establishes stability and derives _a priori_ error estimates. In Section 4, we construct a residual- based _a posteriori_ error indicator and prove its reliability and efficiency. Section 5 reports numerical experiments that confirm the optimal convergence rates and illustrate the performance of the adaptive mesh refinement strategy. Finally, concluding remarks are given in Section 6. ## 2. UnCut FEM for the Poisson equation We consider a hierarchical T-mesh \(\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h\) as the computational background mesh over the rectangular domain \(\hat{\Omega}=[0,1]^d\). A T-mesh facilitates local refinement by permitting T- junctions, which are grid-line endpoints terminating at the midpoint of an adjacent element edge. Following the notation established in \[32\], we define the PHT-spline space over \(\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h\) as \(\mathcal{S}(p,q,\alpha,\beta,\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h):=\left\{s\in C^{\alpha,\beta}(\hat{\Omega})|s|_T\in\mathbb{P}_{p,q}\forall T\in\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h\right\},\) (2.1) where P_p,q_ denotes the space of bivariate tensor-product polynomials of bi-degree (_p,q_) on each element, and \(C^{\alpha,\beta}(\hat{\Omega})\) encodes the prescribed inter-element smoothness. For simplicity, we focus on the symmetric case _p=q_. To ensure global _C_1 continuity and maintain the nestedness of the basis functions during local refinement, it is mathematically required that \(p,q\ge 3\) \[33\]. In this work, we employ the spline space \(\mathcal{S}(k,k,\alpha,\beta,\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h)\), where _k_ denotes the polynomial degree and we set \(p=q=k\ge 3\), ensuring at least _C_1 continuity with \(\alpha,\beta\ge 1\). Some intermediate estimates below are valid already for \(k\ge 2\); however, they are used only under this standing assumption and do not yield a _k_=2 version of the main results. Following the standard hierarchical construction \[2,15\], one obtains a set of global basis functions \(\{R_a\}_{a=1}^{N_a}\subset\mathcal{S}(3,3,1,1,\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h)\), where the dimension _Na_ is directly associated with the number of crossing vertices and T-vertices. For efficient numerical implementation, these basis functions are constructed element-wise via Bézier extraction. Specifically, for each leaf element \(T\in\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h\), there exists an extraction matrix **C**_T_ such that the restriction of the basis functions to _T_ is expressed as a linear combination of the local tensor-product Bernstein basis \(\{B_j\}_{j=1}^{(k+1)^2}\) defined on the reference square \(\hat{T}=[-1,1]^2\). Based on these, we define the discrete space as \(V_h:=\left\{v_h:\hat{\Omega}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}:v_h(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{a=1}^{N_a}v_aR_a(\mathbf{x}),v_a\in\mathbb{R}\right\}.\) (2.2) The space _Vh_ inherits several critical properties for adaptive analysis. First, for \(k\ge 3\), _Vh_ is globally _C_1-continuous, which is particularly advantageous for Galerkin formulations involving second-order operators. Second, the hierarchical structure enables truly local mesh adaptivity while preserving the linear independence of the basis. Consequently, T-junctions do not introduce independent degrees of freedom (DOFs); instead, the extraction operator **C**_T_ implicitly enforces the necessary _C_1 constraints across interfaces of differing refinement levels, ensuring a seamless coupling of the global solution. ### 2.1. Unfitted mesh. Let \(\phi\) be a smooth level-set function, and let \(\phi_h\in V_h\) be a high-order approximation of \(\phi\). We define the discrete interface as \(\Gamma_h:=\{\mathbf{x}:\phi_h(\mathbf{x})=0\}\). Let T_h_ be the submesh of \(\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h\) obtained by discarding all elements whose closures lie entirely outside the discrete domain \(\{\mathbf{x}:\phi_h(\mathbf{x})<0\}\). We define the sets of interior cells and cut (strip) cells by \(\mathcal{T}_h^\mathrm{in}:=\{T\in\mathcal{T}_h:T\cap\Gamma_h=\varnothing\},\)
\(\mathcal{T}_h^\Gamma:=\{T\in\mathcal{T}_h:T\cap\Gamma_h\neq\varnothing\},\)

<tbc>so that \(\mathcal{T}_h=\mathcal{T}_h^\mathrm{in}\cup\mathcal{T}_h^\Gamma\) and \(\mathcal{T}_h^\mathrm{in}\cap\mathcal{T}_h^\Gamma=\emptyset\). Correspondingly, we introduce the open domains

\(\Omega_h^\mathrm{in}:=\big(\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}_h^\mathrm{in}}T\big)^\circ,\Omega_h^\Gamma:=\big(\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}_h^\Gamma} T\big)^\circ,\text{and}\Omega_h:=\big(\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}_h}T\big)^\circ,\)

which satisfy \(\Omega_h^\mathrm{in}\cap\Omega_h^\Gamma=\emptyset\) and \(\Omega_h=\big(\overline{\Omega_h^\mathrm{in}}\cup\overline{\Omega_h^\Gamma}\big)^\circ\). To account for the overlapping supports of the spline basis functions, we further introduce an extended domain \(\widetilde{\Omega}_h\), defined as the union of the supports of all basis functions that intersect \(\Omega_h\), so that \(\Omega_h\subset\widetilde{\Omega}_h\subset\hat{\Omega}\).

Let \(\mathcal{F}_h^\Gamma\) denote the set of interior facets of T_<sub>h</sub>_ that are either intersected by the discrete interface \(\Gamma_h\) or are incident to a cut element. For the hierarchical T-mesh, we denote the diameter of a cell \(T\in\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h\) by _h<sub>T</sub>_, and define the minimum and maximum mesh sizes as

\(h_m:=\mathrm{min}_{T\in\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h}h_T,h_M:=\mathrm{max}_{T\in\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h}h_T,\)

respectively. Throughout the analysis, we set \(h:=h_M=\mathrm{max}_{T\in\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h}h_T\). Figure 1 illustrates the hierarchical T-mesh and the domain partitioning.

**Assumption 2.1.** _We assume that the level-set function_ \(\phi\)_, its approximation_ \(\phi_h\in V_h\)_, and the hierarchical T-mesh satisfy the following properties:_

(P1) \(\phi\in C^{k+1}(\hat{\Omega})\) _and the exact interface is given by_ \(\Gamma:=\{\mathbf{x}\in[0,1]^d:\phi(\mathbf{x})=0\}\)_. There exist constants_ \(\delta_0,c_d,C_d>0\)_, independent of h, such that_<tbc>

<tbc>\(|\nabla\phi(\mathbf{x})|\ge c_d,c_d\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{x},\Gamma)\le|\phi(\mathbf{x})|\le C_d\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{x},\Gamma),\)<tbc>

<tbc>_for all_ \(\mathbf{x}\in U_{\delta_0}(\Gamma)\).<tbc>

(P2) \(\phi_h\in V_h\) _satisfies the following approximation estimates:_<tbc>

\(\|\phi-\phi_h\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}\le Ch^{k+1}\|\phi\|_{H^{k+1}(\widetilde{\Omega}_h)},\) \(\text{(2.3)}\)

\(\|\phi-\phi_h\|_{H^1(\Omega_h)}\le Ch^k\|\phi\|_{H^{k+1}(\widetilde{\Omega}_h)}.\) \(\text{(2.4)}\)

_In addition, the approximation is assumed to satisfy_

\(\|\phi-\phi_h\|_{L^\infty(\hat{\Omega})}+h\|\nabla(\phi-\phi_h)\|_{L^\infty(\hat{\Omega})}+h^2\|D_h^2(\phi-\phi_h)\|_{L^\infty(\hat{\Omega})}\le Ch^{k+1}\|\phi\|_{W^{k+1,\infty}(\hat{\Omega})},\) \(\text{(2.5)}\)

(P3) _The cut-to-interior proximity condition holds: there exists c<sub>b</sub>\>_0 _such that for every_ \(T\in\mathcal{T}_h^\Gamma\)_, there exists an interior element_ \(K\in\mathcal{T}_h^\mathrm{in}\) _satisfying_ \(\mathrm{dist}(T,K)\le c_bh_T\).<tbc>

(P4) _The hierarchical mesh is 1-regular, meaning that the refinement levels of adjacent cells differ by at most one, ensuring that the mesh sizes of neighboring cells are comparable._

**Remark 2.2.** Property (P2) is a standard requirement in the context of unfitted finite element methods, which is naturally satisfied when the _k_-th degree PHT-spline function \(\phi_h\in V_h\) is defined as the global spline interpolation of a sufficiently smooth level-set function \(\phi\). Furthermore, for polynomial degrees \(k\ge 3\), the \(L^\infty\)-norm of \(\nabla\phi_h\) is uniformly bounded as a consequence of (P2) and the standard inverse inequalities for splines.

**Remark 2.3.** Properties (P1)-(P2) ensure that the discrete interface \(\Gamma_h\) provides a high- order approximation of \(\Gamma\) while maintaining its non-degeneracy. Property (P3) serves as a standard geometric assumption, ensuring that every cut cell is sufficiently close to the interior to facilitate the stable extension of the solution. Furthermore, (P4) is critical for guaranteeing that the number of elements _N_ in a face-adjacent path from a cut cell to an interior cell remains uniformly bounded, independent of the local refinement level. This property is essential for establishing the uniform stability of the ghost penalty terms across non-conforming mesh interfaces.

## 2.2. A simple least-squares UnCut FEM using PHT-splines.

In this subsection, we present the proposed numerical scheme and state the main theoretical results. Throughout this paper, the notation \(A\lesssim B\) denotes \(A\le CB\) with a positive constant _C_ independent of the mesh size, while _A≈B_ indicates that \(A\lesssim B\) and \(B\lesssim A\) simultaneously. We utilize \((\cdot,\cdot)_{L^2(D)}\) and \((\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1(D)}\) to denote the standard _L_<sup>2</sup> and _H_<sup>1</sup> inner products over a domain _D_.

Based on the spline space _V<sub>h</sub>_ and the approximate level-set function \(\phi_h\), we define the finite element space as \(S_h:=\{\phi_hv_h:v_h\in V_h\}\). Since the functions in _S<sub>h</sub>_ are globally _C_<sup>1</sup>-continuous, their zero-th and first-order normal jumps across any internal face are intrinsically zero. Thus, the jump penalty term only involves higher-order derivatives from _j_=2 to 2_k_, defined as

\(j_h(u_h,v_h):=\sum_{j=2}^{2k}\sum_{F\in\mathcal{F}_h^\Gamma} h_F^{2j-3}\int_F\left[\left[\partial_n^ju_h\right]\right]\left[\left[\partial_n^jv_h\right]\right],\forall(u_h,v_h)\in S_h\times S_h,\) (2.6)

where _h<sub>F</sub>_:=min(_h_<sub>_T_<sup>+</sup></sub>_,h_<sub>_T_<sup>-</sup></sub>) denotes the characteristic mesh size associated with the interior face \(F=T^+\cap T^-\).

It is important to emphasize that all computations in the proposed scheme (1.3) are carried out directly on the background mesh T_<sub>h</sub>_. This approach circumvents the need for complex numerical integration over geometrically curved cut elements induced by the intersection of the physical boundary with the Cartesian grid. Consequently, the scheme relies solely on standard element-wise quadrature rules, significantly simplifying the implementation and the computational pipeline.

**Theorem 2.4** (_H_<sup>1</sup>-error estimate)**.** _Under Assumption 2.1, assuming_ \(\Omega\subset\Omega_h\)_, let_ \(f\in H^{k-1}(\Omega_h)\) _and let_ \(\tilde{u}\in H^{k+1}(\widetilde{\Omega}_h)\) _be the extension of the exact solution u, satisfying_ \(\tilde{u}|_\Omega=u\) _and_ \(\left\|\tilde{u}\right\|_{H^{k+1}(\widetilde{\Omega}_h)}\le C\left\|u\right\|_{H^{k+1}(\Omega)}\)_. Then the numerical scheme in_ (1.3) _admits a unique solution_ \(u_h\in S_h\)_, and the following error estimate holds:_

\(\left\|\tilde{u}-u_h\right\|_{H^1(\Omega_h)}\le Ch^k\left\|f\right\|_{H^{k-1}(\Omega_h)}.\) (2.7)

Although the hierarchical T-mesh framework permits local refinement, the _a_ priori analysis in Section 3 is carried out under the additional assumption that the active meshes are globally comparable, namely, \(h_M/h_m\le C\) with a constant independent of _h_. Accordingly, we use the

<tbc>global mesh parameter _h_:=_h<sub>M</sub>_ throughout Section 3. The locally refined hierarchical T- meshes considered in Section 4 are investigated from the viewpoint of adaptive computation and are not required to satisfy this global mesh-ratio condition.

## 3. Proof of Theorem 2.4

In this section, we present a detailed error analysis of the proposed scheme (1.3). We first establish several technical preliminaries, including stability and approximation results. We then prove the coercivity and continuity of the associated bilinear form, which ensures the well-posedness of the discrete problem. Finally, in Subsection 3.3, we combine these results to derive the optimal _a priori_ error estimates.

### 3.1. Technical results.

**Lemma 3.1** ( \[19, Lemma 3.6\])**.** _For any integer s with_ \(1\le s\le k+1\) _and any_ \(v\in H^s(\Omega_h)\) _that vanishes in_ \(\Omega\)_, it holds that_<tbc>

\(\|v\|_{L^2(\Omega_h\backslash\Omega)}\le Ch^s\|v\|_{H^s(\Omega_h\backslash\Omega)}.\) (3.1)

<tbc>**Lemma 3.2.** _For any_ \(v_h\in S_h\)_, and two neighboring elements K_<sup>+</sup> _and K_<sup>-</sup> _sharing_ \(F\in\mathcal{F}_h^\Gamma\)_, we have the local estimate_<tbc>

\(\|v_h\|_{H^2(K^+)}^2\le C\big(\|v_h\|_{H^2(K^-)}^2+\sum_{j=2}^{2k}h_F^{2j-3}\|\left[\left[\partial_n^jv_h\right]\right]\|_{L^2(F)}^2\big).\) (3.2)

<tbc>_Proof._ By affine changes of variables, it suffices to establish the estimate on each of the finitely many fixed reference macro-elements \(\widehat{K}=\widehat{K}^+\cup\widehat{K}^-\) arising from the 1-regular hierarchical T-mesh, where \(\widehat{K}^+\) and \(\widehat{K}^-\) share a common edge segment \(\widehat{F}\). Let \(\widehat{n}\) be a fixed unit normal to \(\widehat{F}\). We define the finite-dimensional broken polynomial space of degree 2_k_ on \(\widehat{K}\) as:<tbc>

\(X_k(\widehat{K}):=\{\widehat{p}\in L^2(\widehat{K}):\widehat{p}|_{\widehat{K}^\pm}\in\mathbb{Q}_{2k}(\widehat{K}^\pm)\}.\)

<tbc>For any \(\widehat{p}\in X_k(\widehat{K})\), consider the following functional:

\(N(\widehat{p})^2:=\|\widehat{p}\|_{H^2(\widehat{K}^-)}^2+\sum_{j=0}^{2k}\|\left[\left[\partial_n^j\widehat{p}\right]\right]\|_{L^2(\widehat{F})}^2.\)

We first show that \(N(\cdot)\) defines a norm on \(X_k(\widehat{K})\). Suppose \(N(\widehat{p})=0\). The vanishing of the first term implies \(\widehat{p}\equiv 0\) on \(\widehat{K}^-\), which further ensures that all its derivative traces vanish on \(\widehat{F}\) from the side of \(\widehat{K}^-\). The vanishing of the jump terms \(\left[\left[\partial_n^j\widehat{p}\right]\right]=0\) for _j_=0_,...,_2_k_ then strictly forces \(\partial_n^j\widehat{p}^+=0\) on \(\widehat{F}\) for _j_=0_,...,_2_k_. Since \(\widehat{p}|_{\widehat{K}^+}\) has degree at most 2_k_ in the direction normal to \(\widehat{F}\), and we have 2_k_+1 homogeneous conditions on the normal derivatives along the edge \(\widehat{F}\), the factor theorem implies that \(\widehat{p}\) must be identically zero on \(\widehat{K}^+\). Thus \(N(\cdot)\) is a valid norm on \(X_k(\widehat{K})\).

By the equivalence of norms in finite-dimensional spaces, \(N(\cdot)\) dominates the \(H^2(\widehat{K}^+)\)- norm. For our specific discrete function \(v_h\in S_h\), the global _C_<sup>1</sup>-continuity implies \(\left[\left[\partial_n^0v_h\right]\right]=0\) and \(\left[\left[\partial_n^1v_h\right]\right]=0\), which allows the jump summation to effectively start from _j_=2.

Finally, using \(h_{K^+}\simeq h_{K^-}\simeq h_F\) and the affine scaling relations

\(|v_h|_{H^m(K)}^2\simeq h_F^{d-2m}|\widehat{v}_h|_{H^m(\widehat{K})}^2,\left[\left[\left[\partial_n^jv_h\right]\right]\right]\left|\right|_{L^2(F)}^2\simeq h_F^{d-1-2j}\left[\left[\left[\partial_n^j\widehat{v}_h\right]\right]\right]\left|\right|_{L^2(\widehat{F})}^2,\)

we obtain the factor \(h_F^{2j-3}\) and hence (3.2). □

**Lemma 3.3** (Stability property)**.** _For any_ \(v_h\in S_h\)_, we have the following stability estimate_

\(\|v_h\|_{H^2(\Omega_h)}^2\le C\big(\|\Delta v_h\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}^2+j_h(v_h,v_h)\big).\) (3.3)

_Proof._ Let \(K\in\mathcal{T}_h^\Gamma\) be a cut element. By Remark 2.3, there exists a path of elements \(K=K_0,K_1,\dots,K_N\) such that \(K_N\in\mathcal{T}_h^\mathrm{in}\) and, for each _i_=1_,...,N_, the elements _K__i_-1 and _Ki_ share a common face \(F_i\in\mathcal{F}_h^\Gamma\). **Require:** Error tolerance TOL_\>_0, marking parameter \(\theta\in(0,1)\), and maximum iteration limit \(\ell_\mathrm{max}>0\).

1: **Initialize:** Construct an initial uniform background mesh \(\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h^{(0)}\) with \(N_0\times N_0\) cells. Set \(\ell\leftarrow 0\) and \(\eta^{(0)}\leftarrow+\infty\).

2: **while** \(\eta^{(\ell)}>\) TOL and \(\ell\le\ell_\mathrm{max}\) **do**

3: **Step 1:** From the background mesh \(\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h^{(\ell)}\) construct the active mesh \(\mathcal{T}_h^{(\ell)}\subset\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h^{(\ell)}\) based on the current level-set function \(\phi_h^{(\ell)}\).

4: **Step 2:** Assemble the discrete system on \(\mathcal{T}_h^{(\ell)}\) and solve the resulting linear system to obtain \(u_h^{(\ell)}\).

5: **Step 3:** Compute the local indicators \(\eta_T^{(\ell)}=\|\Delta u_h^{(\ell)}+f\|_{L^2(T)}\) for \(T\in\mathcal{T}_h^{(\ell)}\), and the global indicator \(\eta^{(\ell)}:=\left(\sum_{T\in\mathcal{T}_h^{(\ell)}}(\eta_T^{(\ell)})^2\right)^{1/2}\).

6: **Step 4:** Find a minimal set of marked cells \(\mathcal{M}^{(\ell)}\subset\mathcal{T}_h^{(\ell)}\) such that

\(\sum_{T\in\mathcal{M}^{(\ell)}}(\eta_T^{(\ell)})^2\ge\theta\sum_{T\in\mathcal{T}_h^{(\ell)}}(\eta_T^{(\ell)})^2=\theta\big(\eta^{(\ell)}\big)^2.\)

7: **Step 5:** Apply one-to-four (one-to-eight in 3D) subdivision to each marked cell \(T\in\mathcal{M}^{(\ell)}\) and recursively refine the necessary neighboring cells to strictly enforce the 1-regular constraint. This process yields the valid hierarchical refined mesh \(\hat{\mathcal{T}}_h^{(\ell+1)}\).

8: **Update:** Set \(\ell\leftarrow\ell+1\).

9: **end while**

the active computational mesh \(\mathcal{T}_h^{(\ell+1)}\) is dynamically identified by selecting the elements intersecting the discrete domain \(\{\phi_h^{(\ell+1)}<0\}\).

## 5. Numerical experiments

All numerical experiments are implemented using the MATLAB-based package `IGAPack` \[2\], employing the hierarchical T-mesh described in the previous sections. Unless otherwise specified, we utilize bicubic PHT-splines (polynomial degree _k_=3) for the discrete space _V<sub>h</sub>_. In the following tests, we take tolerance TOL=10<sup>-8</sup>, marking parameter \(\theta=0.25\) and maximum iteration \(\ell_\mathrm{max}=20\) in Algorithm 1.

### 5.1. Example 1.

We consider a smooth level-set function,

\(\phi(x,y)=(x-0.5)^2+(y-0.5)^2-r^2,(x,y)\in(0,1)^2,\) (5.1)

with _r_=0.3. The exact solution is chosen as \(u_\mathrm{ex}(x,y)=\phi(x,y)\mathrm{exp}(x+y)\), and the corresponding right-hand side is computed analytically. Here _u_<sub>ex</sub> is explicitly defined on the entire background domain \(\hat{\Omega}\), so the errors evaluated on \(\Omega_h\) involve this fixed extension and have no extension ambiguity.

We consider uniformly refined meshes, starting from an initial coarse mesh consisting of \(16\times 16\) cells. These meshes do not contain hanging nodes and satisfy _h<sub>M</sub>/h<sub>m</sub>_=1. The accuracy is evaluated by computing the errors \(\|u_h-u_\mathrm{ex}\|_{H^1(\Omega_h)}\) and \(\|u_h-u_\mathrm{ex}\|_{H^2(\Omega_h)}\) on the background mesh. As reported in  1, the proposed method achieves the optimal convergence rates predicted by the theory: O(_h_<sup>3</sup>) in the _H_<sup>1</sup>-norm and O(_h_<sup>2</sup>) in the _H_<sup>2</sup>-norm.

### 5.2. Example 2.

Consider the shifted coordinates \(X:=x-\frac{1}{2}\), \(Y:=y-\frac{1}{2}\) with the level-set function:

\(\phi(x,y):=X^2+Y^2-r_0^2-A\sum_{j=0}^5\mathrm{exp}\big(-\frac{(X-X_j)^2+(Y-Y_j)^2}{\sigma_0^2}\big),\) (5.2)

<tbc>where the bump centers (_X<sub>j</sub>,Y<sub>j</sub>_) are distributed on a circle of radius _r_<sub>0</sub>,

\((X_j,Y_j):=\big(r_0cos\theta_j,r_0sin\theta_j\big),\theta_j:=\frac{2\pi j}{6},j=0,\dots,5.\) (5.3)

Let \(u_\text{base}(x,y):=exp\big(-\frac{(x-0.3)^2+(y-0.7)^2}{\sigma^2}\big)\), we prescribe the exact solution \(u_\text{ex}(x,y):=\phi(x,y)u_\text{base}\). In this test, we take _r_<sub>0</sub>=0.2, \(\sigma_0=0.1\), _A_=0.5 and \(\sigma=0.06\).

Starting from an initial \(32\times 32\) background mesh, we compare the performance of uniform refinement against the proposed adaptive strategy. Fig. 2 illustrates the evolution of the indicator \(\eta\) and the exact errors with respect to the active DOFs. While both strategies successfully achieve the optimal asymptotic rates (O(_h_<sup>3</sup>) in _H_<sup>1</sup>-norm and O(_h_<sup>2</sup>) in _H_<sup>2</sup>- norm), the adaptive method drastically reduces the computational cost.

The superior efficiency is further quantified in  2. The adaptive approach attains an accuracy level comparable to that of uniform refinement using nearly 60% fewer DOFs (6128 vs. 14764). Conversely, for a fixed DOF budget, adaptivity reduces the numerical error by almost an order of magnitude. This targeted efficiency is visually confirmed in Fig. 3; the generated adaptive T-mesh (3328 leaf cells) automatically concentrates the refinement in the local region \([0.2,0.5]\times[0.5,0.8]\) to strictly resolve the sharp peak at (0.3,0.7), demonstrating the robustness of the _a posteriori_ indicator.

## 6. Conclusion

We proposed and analyzed a least-squares UnCut FEM for the Poisson problem on level- set domains. The method combines a \(\phi\)-FEM unfitted construction with _C_<sup>1</sup> continuous PHT-splines, which enables a fully primal formulation based on the _L_<sup>2</sup> residual \(\|\Delta u_h+f\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}\). All terms are assembled on the active background domain \(\Omega_h\) using standard element-wise quadrature, thereby avoiding geometric integration over curved boundaries or cut subregions of boundary elements. Consequently, the method is simple to implement and computationally efficient. We proved existence and uniqueness of the discrete solution and
